newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Three killed as South African Zulus march.
newsitem.headline: Three killed as South African Zulus march.

text.p: Three people were killed and at least four wounded on Wednesday as Zulu nationalists marched to commemorate the slaying of more than 50 people in a 1994 protest ahead of South Africa's first all-race election.
Police said the first two killings occurred in Soweto black township before the rally, while the third was reported soon after the protesters had arrived in Johannesburg's city centre.
Reports that violent clashes had erupted between police and demonstrators afterwards were denied by police on the scene.
"We confirm three deaths. Two people were killed in Soweto township and one at the station in town," police Sergeant Mark Reynolds told Reuters.

The march was held to commemorate the deaths of at least 55 people as well as the hundreds injured in and around Johannesburg during the 1994 demonstration when supporters of the mainly Zulu-based Inkatha Freedom Party marched in support of Zulu King Goodwill Zwelithini.

Razor wire protected the front of the headquarters of President Nelson Mandela's African National Congress (ANC), where eight Zulu demonstrators were killed by security guards during the 1994 pre-election march.

Violence first erupted on Wednesday in the sprawling Soweto township outside Johannesburg early in the morning when gunshots were fired from various workers hostels and roads were barricaded with rocks.
Two people were also wounded in separate shootings near the hostels and two buses were burnt.

Then in the afternoon sporadic shootings occurred after speeches during the commemoration protest by about 12,000 marchers -- most of them in traditional Zulu dress and carrying spears, sticks and leather-bound shields.
As the marchers dispersed from the city centre, shots were again fired into the air.
"We have no reports of police firing back at the marchers. They are dispersing relatively peacefully," Reynolds said.
Police said some of the demonstrators and bystanders had attempted to loot shops as they made their way home.
Organisers said the march was not only to remember the dead, but was also a call on the government to declare the day a public holiday.
Mandela told parliament months after the 1994 shootings that he had ordered security guards to protect the ANC building against any attack.
The attorney-general launched a probe into the killings, but no one has yet been prosecuted.
Market traders said earlier news of the killings had weakened the rand and local bonds. But markets calmed later as dealers digested Finance Minister Trevor Manuel's maiden budget.
